# Wound healing

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Surgery > Preoperative and postoperative care > Wound healing*

[Original Article Link](/library/Kh0UUf)

---

## Summary

Wounds are a break in the <u>skin</u> and/or a disruption of the <u>skin</u>'s normal barrier function. Wound healing is a step-wise cellular response involving <u>fibroblasts</u>, <u>macrophages</u>, <u>endothelial</u> cells, and <u>keratinocytes</u> that restore the structural and functional integrity of the <u>skin</u>. The four general stages of wound healing are <u>exudative</u>, resorptive, proliferative, and maturation. While the three initial stages take place within the first two weeks, the last stage proceeds over months. Many factors affect wound healing, including the size of the wound, tension on wound edges, the presence of foreign bodies or infection, and the baseline health and nutrition of the patient. In addition, chronic health conditions such as <u>diabetes</u> and <u>peripheral vascular disease</u> can slow the wound healing process. <u>Delayed wound healing</u> may lead to the formation of a <u>chronic wound</u>.

| <br>Resorptive  <br> | <br>* Days 1–3<br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Chemotaxis</u> (via PAF, <u>PDGF</u>, and <u>TGF-β</u>) of inflammatory cells (i.e., <u>neutrophils</u>, <u>macrophages</u>, <u>lymphocytes</u>) to the site of injury <br><br>* <u>Macrophages</u> release growth factors and <u>cytokines</u> that recruit other <u>immune cells</u>, stimulate <u>fibroblast</u> <u>proliferation</u> (<u>fibrosis</u>) and resorb debris.<br><br>* <u>Lymphocytes</u> migrate to injury approx. 72 hours after the injury to promote <u>cellular immunity</u>.<br><br>* Continued <u>vasodilation</u><br><br>* <u>EGF</u> induces <u>tyrosine kinases</u> such as <u>EGFR</u> → <u>epithelium</u> at wound margins begins to proliferate<br><br><br> | <br><br>* PAF<br><br>* <u>PDGF</u><br><br>* <u>TGF-β</u><br><br><br> |  |
| <br>Proliferative  <br> | <br>* Days 3–7<br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Macrophages</u><br><br>* <u>Fibroblasts</u><br><br>* <u>Myofibroblasts</u>,<br><br>* <u>Endothelial</u> cells<br><br>* <u>Keratinocytes</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* Formation of granulation tissue <br><br>* <u>Fibroplasia</u>  → synthesis and deposition of <u>type III collagen</u>.<br><br>* Growth factors (FGF, <u>EGF</u>, <u>VEGF</u>, <u>PDGF</u>, and <u>TGF-β</u>) from <u>fibroblasts</u> and <u>epithelial</u> cells promote <u>angiogenesis</u>.<br><br>* <u>PDGF</u> stimulates <u>smooth muscle cell</u> migration and <u>fibroblast</u> growth → <u>collagen synthesis</u><br><br>* Wound contraction occurs as <u>collagen synthesis</u> increases and pulls the wound edges together. This process is facilitated by <u>myofibroblasts</u>.<br><br>* <u>Epidermal</u> cells<br><br>* Migrate across the <u>collagen</u> matrix to form a full layer<br><br>* Secrete <u>collagenase</u> to dissolve the clot<br><br>* Replicate along a provisional matrix formed by inflammatory cells to completely cover the wound<br><br><br> | <br><br>* FGF<br><br>* <u>EGF</u><br><br>* <u>PDGF</u><br><br>* <u>VEGF</u><br><br>* <u>TGF-β</u><br><br><br> |
| <br>Maturation <br> | <br>* Weeks to 1 year<br><br> | <br>* <u>Fibroblasts</u><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Scar</u> forms with the <u>proliferation</u> of <u>fibroblasts</u> and remodeling of <u>connective tissue</u>.<br><br>* Removal of excess <u>collagen</u><br><br>* <u>Macrophages</u> release matrix metalloproteinases and <u>collagenases</u> (require <u>zinc</u>), which facilitate the final remodeling of <u>type III collagen</u> into <u>type I collagen</u>.<br><br>* <u>Collagen</u> becomes more organized, returning strength to the region of injury.<br><br>* Peak tensile strength (∼ 80% of original strength)  is reached ∼ 60 days after injury.<br><br>* Sweat and <u>sebaceous glands</u> do not regenerate.<br><br><br> | <br>* <u>Matrix metalloproteinase</u><br><br> |

## Wound healing complications

### <u>Scar</u> formation




* Occurs when initial injury cannot be repaired solely by cell <u>regeneration</u>

* Cells that cannot be regenerated (e.g., due to chronic injury or because acute injury is too severe) are replaced by <u>connective tissue</u>.

* After 3 months, 70–80% of tensile strength is regained. [[2]](/library/tLbXz8)

* Maximum strength of <u>scar</u> tissue is approx. 80% of that of unwounded <u>skin</u>. [[2]](/library/tLbXz8)





### Excessive <u>scar</u>




* Dysregulation of the wound healing process during the proliferative stage and maturation stage leads to excess <u>fibroblast</u> replication and <u>collagen</u> deposition.

* Molecular mechanisms [[3]](/library/iRXJ5B)[[4]](/library/QRXu5B)[[5]](/library/jRX_5B)[[6]](/library/PRXWMB)[[7]](/library/4RX3MB)[[8]](/library/kRXmMB)

* Increased production of:

* Certain isoforms of <u>transforming growth factor-beta</u> (primary mediator)

* <u>Connective tissue growth factor</u>

* <u>Platelet-derived growth factor</u>

* <u>Tissue inhibitors of metalloproteinases</u>

* Decreased production of:

* Basic <u>fibroblast</u> growth factor

* <u>Metalloproteinases</u> (e.g., <u>collagenase</u>)

* <u>Interleukin-10</u>





#### <u>Hypertrophic scar</u>




* Cutaneous condition characterized by high <u>fibroblast</u> <u>proliferation</u> and <u>collagen</u> production that leads to a raised <u>scar</u> that does not grow beyond the boundaries of the original lesion.

* See “<u>Hypertrophic scars</u>.”





#### <u>Keloid</u>




* <u>Skin</u> lesions caused by high <u>fibroblast</u> <u>proliferation</u> and <u>collagen</u> production in excessive tissue response to typically small <u>skin</u> injuries

* Lesions grow beyond the original wound margins, leading to a ”claw-like” appearance.

* See “<u>Keloid scars</u>.”





### <u>Contracture</u>




* Excessive <u>proliferation</u> in <u>myofibroblasts</u> during proliferative and maturation phases leads to contraction of the wound.

* Excessive contraction can reduce the functionality of the injured limbs or organs.

* Wounds that cross a <u>joint</u> (e.g., on the hands and fingers) are at high risk for causing functional deficits from <u>contracture</u>. Periodic exercise of the involved limb can help preserve normal function.
